solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Polymath about to abandon snake markets (10)

indicatorNotes.to abandon: the ON leaves the snake's name

blocks.note: an agora is a Greek marketplace

annotation.surface: A learned all-rounder quits the snake trade.
annotation.walkthrough: 'About' is ON, not the usual C or RE, and it is the ON that leaves PYTHON. The Greek markets suit the Greek mathematician.
annotation.definitionFit: Pythagoras was mathematician, philosopher and mystic: a polymath.

entries.clue: Shade of dark grey, essentially (5)

blocks.note: an old colour name for a dark greyish-blue
a two-word Latin phrase meaning 'in itself', run together

annotation.surface: Someone describing a colour as, at heart, dark grey.
annotation.walkthrough: The enumeration (5) hides that the second meaning is the two-word Latin phrase per se.
annotation.definitionFit: Perse is a dark grey or greyish-blue colour, mostly found in older literature.

entries.clue: Overly suggestive of Siam, porcelain’s reportedly phoney (3-6)

indicatorNotes.reportedly: what is reported is heard, so the sound counts

blocks.note: Siam is the old name of Thailand
Ming porcelain, from the Chinese dynasty

annotation.surface: A dealer's supposedly Siamese porcelain turns out to be a fake.
annotation.walkthrough: Said aloud, 'too Thai Ming' is two-timing. The 's reads as 'is', joining wordplay to definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A two-timing lover is false, deceitful: phoney.

entries.clue: Quick as the sandpiper flies? (2,1,4,2,5)

blocks.note: one kind of sandpiper shares its name with the nautical unit of speed

annotation.surface: A birdwatcher admiring how fast a sandpiper flies.
annotation.walkthrough: The knot is a wading bird of the sandpiper family, and knots are also a unit of speed; the idiom 'at a rate of knots' means very fast.
annotation.definitionFit: At a rate of knots is a British idiom for very quickly.

entries.clue: Covertly displacing crown, won’t ambassador question groundless treason? (2,3,2)

indicatorNotes.displacing crown: the crown of a down word is its top letter, here W
indicatorNotes.groundless: ground means reason, so REASON comes out

annotation.surface: An envoy asks whether an unfounded plot to unseat the monarch is being kept secret.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Crown' and 'treason' make you think of royalty, but the crown is just W, and 'ground' is a synonym for reason.
annotation.definitionFit: On the QT (quiet) means secretly, covertly.

entries.clue: First of samples in song’s Led Zeppelin? (7)

indicatorNotes.First of: takes the first letter of samples
indicatorNotes.Led: the song's piece has led, coming first

annotation.surface: A music fan spotting a sample of a Led Zeppelin track in a new song.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Led Zeppelin' reads as the band, but split apart: 'Led' says the song part goes first, and 'Zeppelin' alone is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A zeppelin is a rigid airship, named after Count Zeppelin.

entries.clue: Napoleon’s rank Suchet ultimately took back (4)

indicatorNotes.ultimately: takes the last letter of Suchet
indicatorNotes.back: the whole thing runs right to left

annotation.surface: Marshal Suchet, one of Napoleon's generals, finally takes back his rank.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Napoleon's' signals French. Suchet was a real Napoleonic marshal, which makes the surface convincing.
annotation.definitionFit: A French word: in old France the three estates of the realm, ranks of society, were the états.

entries.clue: Runs with redirected tour around city (5)

indicatorNotes.redirected: the letters of TOUR take a new route
indicatorNotes.around: the shuffled TOUR goes round R

blocks.note: R = runs in cricket, placed inside

annotation.surface: A rerouted tour bus circling a town.
annotation.walkthrough: TRUO wraps R after its third letter: TRU(R)O. Truro is the cathedral city of Cornwall.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Cornwall's only city, with its cathedral.

entries.clue: What kidnappers may do is disagree (4,5)

blocks.note: the everyday idiom for objecting to a point

annotation.surface: A deadpan remark about what kidnapping amounts to.
annotation.walkthrough: Issue is an old legal word for children, so kidnappers literally take issue.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: the idiom for objecting, and literally seizing someone's offspring.

entries.clue: Go out of one’s mind, according to faculty? (14)

annotation.surface: Someone going out of their mind, perhaps over university faculty politics.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Go out of one's mind' reads as an idiom for losing your sanity; split it into two literal parts.
annotation.definitionFit: A university faculty is a department, so departmentally means by faculty.

entries.clue: Words of warning with which the 2016 Games were diplomatically secured? (4,3)

blocks.note: the 2016 Olympics were held in Rio de Janeiro

annotation.surface: A reflection on the tact needed to pull off the 2016 Olympics.
annotation.walkthrough: The enumeration splits the answer at a different point from the wordplay. The Riot Act was an old British law read aloud to order crowds to disperse.
annotation.definitionFit: To read someone the riot act is to give them a severe warning.

entries.clue: Stag fight in East London reported by Spooner (7)

indicatorNotes.reported by Spooner: Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words

blocks.note: Bow is a district of London's East End; it takes the R sound from its partner
a ruck is a brawl; it takes the B sound from Bow

annotation.surface: A news story about a stag do brawl in the East End.
annotation.walkthrough: The fight comes first in the clue but the place leads in the phrase that gets swapped: a ruck in Bow is a Bow ruck.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the male of the roe deer is a stag.

entries.clue: Bessie expanded Hazel Nuts with Bite (9)

indicatorNotes.Nuts: crazy, so the letters are scrambled

annotation.surface: Reads like a product name: Bessie's brand of hazelnuts with bite.
annotation.walkthrough: The capitals dress it up as a brand; ignore them. Bessie is a pet form of Elizabeth, and 'expanded' asks for the full name.
annotation.definitionFit: Bessie is short for Elizabeth; written out in full, it is Elizabeth.

entries.clue: Every second of May, if only in Mayo (5)

indicatorNotes.Every second of: take the 2nd, 4th, 6th letters and so on

annotation.surface: Someone longing for the month of May in County Mayo.
annotation.walkthrough: Mayo looks like the Irish county, but it is short for mayonnaise.
annotation.definitionFit: Mayo is short for mayonnaise, and this Provençal garlic sauce is a kind of it.

entries.clue: Cream that’s low on additives? (5)

blocks.note: the cream = the best of a group
additives are E numbers; 'lite' is marketing spelling for low

annotation.surface: A food label boasting a cream with few additives.
annotation.walkthrough: E numbers are the codes for food additives in Europe, so a product with few of them is E-lite.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: the pick of society, and a jokey E-LITE label for food light on E numbers.

entries.clue: Having engaged new principal, they adapted style of governance (9)

indicatorNotes.Having engaged: the rearranged THEY takes NARCH inside
indicatorNotes.adapted: something adapted has been altered to fit, so THEY's letters are rearranged

blocks.note: arch = chief, principal, as in arch-enemy

annotation.surface: A school that has hired a new head and changed how it is run.
annotation.walkthrough: 'New principal' looks like a headteacher, but it is two parts, N + ARCH, going inside ETH…Y.
annotation.definitionFit: An ethnarchy is rule by an ethnarch, a governor of a people or province.

entries.clue: Officers provide recommendation for county (9)

blocks.note: Staffs is the abbreviation for Staffordshire, an English county

annotation.surface: Police officers giving advice to a county council.
annotation.walkthrough: A tipstaff is a court officer, named for the metal-tipped staff once carried.
annotation.definitionFit: Tipstaffs are officers of a law court, like sheriff's officers.

entries.clue: Choices for sweet couple with finale of Brief Encounter? (5,4)

blocks.note: a fool is a fruit-and-cream dessert

annotation.surface: A pudding menu for a couple watching the film Brief Encounter.
annotation.walkthrough: Brief Encounter is a famous British film, but here it means a very short chess game: fool's mate is the quickest possible checkmate.
annotation.definitionFit: Fool's mate ends a chess game in two moves: the finale of a brief encounter.

entries.clue: His welcoming Henry with fine sporting show? (4,5)

annotation.definition: His welcoming Henry with fine sporting show?

indicatorNotes.welcoming: a host welcoming guests takes them inside, so HIS holds the rest
indicatorNotes.sporting: to sport something is to wear it, so GIVE wears H and F inside

blocks.note: give = show, as in give signs
H = henry, the unit of inductance

annotation.surface: A man greets Henry with a fine display of sportsmanship.
annotation.walkthrough: Henry is the unit of inductance and fine is the pencil grade, so each gives one letter. Read straight, the whole clue pictures a man greeting Henry with a palm-slap.
annotation.definitionFit: The whole clue is the picture: a high five is the raised-palm slap with which a player welcomes a teammate.

entries.clue: Caller, please confirm five gold rings (7)

indicatorNotes.rings: as a verb, to ring is to encircle, so V and OR go round IS IT

annotation.surface: A radio caller checking the 'five gold rings' line from The Twelve Days of Christmas.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Five gold rings' is the carol line, but here 'rings' is a verb: V…OR go round IS IT.
annotation.definitionFit: A caller is someone who visits, a visitor.

entries.clue: A little bit tense after members set up gym (7)

indicatorNotes.after: placed after in time means written later, so T goes at the end
indicatorNotes.set up: in a down clue, set up means written upwards

annotation.surface: A gym member slightly tense after the club has been set up.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Members' looks like club members, but it means limbs: pins is slang for legs.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: something snipped off is a small fragment.

entries.clue: Play absconding lovers in Handel opera (5)

indicatorNotes.in: the answer sits inside the words that follow

annotation.surface: A plot summary of a Handel opera about lovers who run away.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition is a whole phrase: to elope is to act the part of lovers running off together.
annotation.definitionFit: To elope is to run away secretly to marry, as absconding lovers do.

entries.clue: Pasty, at an appropriate time, and whiskey to go (5)

indicatorNotes.to go: as in a takeaway order, the whiskey is to go, so W leaves

blocks.note: as when = at the fitting moment
W (whiskey in the NATO alphabet) removed

annotation.surface: Pastries eaten at the right moment, washed down with whisky to take away.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pasty' looks like the Cornish pastry, but it is the adjective for pale.
annotation.definitionFit: Ashen means pale, pasty-faced.

entries.clue: Healing involved getting this woman in (5)

indicatorNotes.involved: entangled, so the letters are mixed

blocks.note: HEALING with I and N set aside
IN is the part the mystery woman is joined by to make HEALING

annotation.surface: A healing process that required bringing a certain woman in.
annotation.walkthrough: Reverse logic: HEALING is an anagram of the answer plus IN, so strip IN from it and rearrange the rest.
annotation.definitionFit: Helga is a woman's name; 'this woman' points at the answer itself.

entries.clue: Son with least money checks for reaction (4,5)

blocks.note: skint is British slang for broke

annotation.surface: The poorest son in a family being tested for his reaction.
annotation.walkthrough: SKINTEST, the most skint, comes first and S is added on.
annotation.definitionFit: A medical term: allergists prick or patch the skin and watch it for a reaction.

entries.clue: Very healthy, having shifted old bulge (5)

indicatorNotes.having shifted: to shift something is to move it away, so O is moved out of the phrase

annotation.surface: A dieter delighted to have lost an old paunch.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Very healthy' reads as the definition, but it is wordplay; SWELL here is the verb or noun for bulge.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, as noun or verb: a swelling bulges.

entries.clue: Computer section after grant to back business flyer (7)

indicatorNotes.after: coming after means written later, so IT goes at the end
indicatorNotes.to back: a backer stands behind, so LET is placed behind CO

annotation.surface: A business applying for an IT department grant.
annotation.walkthrough: The bird is usually spelt coal tit; cole tit is an accepted variant, and the wordplay insists on it.
annotation.definitionFit: A cole tit is a small bird: a flyer.

entries.clue: Writer’s written about open country by fell (7)

indicatorNotes.written about: the writer is written round the rest, so POE's letters surround it

blocks.note: by = times = X, as in 3 by 4

annotation.surface: An author writes about moorland beside a fell.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fell' looks like the northern English word for a hill, but it is the verb, to knock down.
annotation.definitionFit: Named after the slaughterman's axe: to poleaxe is to knock someone down in one blow.

entries.clue: Fellow students heading off without looking at the score (4)

indicatorNotes.heading off: the head of a word is its first letter, and it is taken off

blocks.note: playing by ear, not reading the music

annotation.surface: Students heading out to play without their sheet music.
annotation.walkthrough: The score is sheet music, not a sports result.
annotation.definitionFit: Your year is the students in the same school cohort.

entries.clue: All but striking oil here? (6,4)

blocks.note: an oil well is where oil is struck

annotation.surface: A prospector wondering whether this is the spot to strike oil.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Striking oil' reads as one phrase, but striking means good-looking.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both phrases mean almost, nearly.
